title: FDA Drug Safety Communication: Important safety label changes to cholesterol-lowering statin drugs
journal: US Food and Drug Administration, Drug Safety Communication, 28 February 2012
result: Labels of all statins were revised. Routine periodic liver enzyme monitoring was removed; testing is advised before starting and as clinically indicated. In the Adverse Event Reporting System the reporting rate of serious statin-associated liver injury was 2 or fewer per million patient-years; of 75 cases of severe liver injury, death or transplantation reported to 2009 (27 severe injury, 37 deaths, 11 transplants), 30 (14 deaths, 7 transplants, 9 severe injury) were assessed as possibly or probably associated with a statin and none as highly likely or definite. Of 133 patients with idiosyncratic drug-induced acute liver failure in the Acute Liver Failure Study Group, 15 were taking statins, and in 6 a statin was the only potential cause. Rare postmarketing reports of cognitive impairment (memory loss, forgetfulness, amnesia, confusion) were added: reports generally described people over 50 with ill-defined memory loss, onset 1 day to years after exposure, reversal on discontinuation with median resolution 3 weeks, and no association with fixed or progressive dementia, statin, age, dose or concomitant drugs; observational studies and trials did not suggest common or clinically significant cognitive decline. Increases in HbA1c and fasting glucose were added, based on a 27% increase in investigator-reported diabetes with rosuvastatin in JUPITER, the meta-analysis by Sattar et al. of 13 trials with 91,140 participants (odds ratio 1.09, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.17) and that by Rajpathak et al. of 6 trials with 57,593 participants (relative risk 1.13, 1.03 to 1.23). FDA stated that it continues to believe the cardiovascular benefits outweigh these small increased risks.
